points: Glass beads with particle diameter 0.5 mm packed in a column with bed length 1.2 m and internal diameter 0.05 m
Void fraction of the packed bed was 0.42
Water at 25 °C was the fluid
Superficial velocity ranged from 0.01 m/s to 0.08 m/s
Pressure drop was 0.8 kPa at the lowest superficial velocity and 18.4 kPa at the highest superficial velocity
Ergun equation prediction at the highest superficial velocity was 17.1 kPa, and the measured value exceeded the prediction by 7.6 %
Repeat measurement comprised 3 runs at each superficial velocity; standard deviation of pressure drop at the highest superficial velocity was 0.3 kPa
definitions: superficial velocity = volumetric flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area, in metres per second
pressure drop = pressure difference between the bed inlet and the bed outlet, in kilopascals
void fraction = void volume divided by total bed volume, dimensionless
limits: Comparison covers water as the fluid and a single particle size; no gas flow and no second particle size were tested
Wall channeling was not measured directly
figures: Fig. 1: pressure drop against superficial velocity for the packed bed
prose: The packed bed contained glass beads with a particle diameter of 0.5 mm in a column with a bed length of 1.2 m and an internal diameter of 0.05 m. Void fraction, the void volume divided by the total bed volume, was 0.42 for the packed bed. Water at 25 °C flowed upward through the packed bed, and pressure drop, the pressure difference between the bed inlet and the bed outlet, was recorded at each set flow rate. Superficial velocity, the volumetric flow rate divided by the empty-column cross-sectional area, covered the range from 0.01 m/s to 0.08 m/s. Pressure drop was 0.8 kPa at the lowest superficial velocity. Pressure drop reached 18.4 kPa at the highest superficial velocity. Fig. 1 shows pressure drop against superficial velocity across the full range, and the curve bends upward as superficial velocity rises. The upward bend marks the growing share of inertial resistance in the packed bed, since viscous resistance alone gives a straight line through the origin. The Ergun equation, a correlation that adds a viscous term and an inertial term for flow through packed beds, gave a prediction of 17.1 kPa at the highest superficial velocity. The measured pressure drop exceeded the Ergun prediction by 7.6 % at the highest superficial velocity. The excess sits in the range where the inertial term carries most of the resistance, and a small error in void fraction moves the inertial term more than the viscous term. Repeat measurement comprised 3 runs at each superficial velocity, and the standard deviation of pressure drop at the highest superficial velocity was 0.3 kPa. Scatter at lower velocities stayed within the resolution of the pressure taps, and no run showed drift during a measurement set. The agreement between the measured pressure drop and the Ergun prediction holds for water as the fluid and for the single particle size in the packed bed, and the comparison does not extend to gas flow or to a bed with a second particle size. Channeling along the column wall remains a possible source of the excess at the highest velocity, and a bed with a larger column-to-particle diameter ratio would test that source.

points: Batch reactor with liquid volume 2 L held at 70 °C, well mixed, with no inflow and no outflow during the batch
Initial concentration of reactant 0.80 mol/L
First-order rate constant 0.045 per minute
Batch time 60 minutes: product of rate constant and time 2.7; remaining fraction of reactant 0.067; conversion 93.3 %
Half-life check: natural logarithm term 0.693 divided by the rate constant gives 15.4 minutes; conversion at the half-life 50 %
Shorter batch time 20 minutes: product of rate constant and time 0.9; conversion 59.3 %
definitions: X = conversion, amount of reactant consumed divided by the initial amount of reactant, dimensionless
k = first-order rate constant, proportionality constant between reaction rate and concentration, in per minute
concentration = amount of reactant per unit volume of liquid, in moles per litre
limits: Rate constant applies at the stated temperature; a temperature change changes the rate constant
Balance assumes constant liquid volume and a well-mixed reactor
prose: Conversion in a batch reactor follows from a mole balance on the reacting species, and this tutorial computes conversion for a first-order reaction from the rate constant and the batch time. The batch reactor holds a liquid volume of 2 L at 70 °C, with no inflow and no outflow during the batch, and the contents are well mixed. Conversion, written as the symbol X, is the amount of reactant consumed divided by the initial amount of reactant, and conversion is dimensionless. The initial concentration of reactant is 0.80 mol/L. The rate constant, written as the symbol k, is the proportionality constant between reaction rate and concentration for a first-order reaction, with units of per minute, and the worked example uses a rate constant of 0.045 per minute. The mole balance for a well-mixed batch reactor sets accumulation of reactant equal to consumption by reaction, and integration gives a remaining fraction equal to the exponential of the negative product of the rate constant and the time. A batch time of 60 minutes gives a product of 2.7, and the exponential of the negative product is 0.067. Conversion at the batch time is the amount consumed divided by the initial amount, and conversion reaches 93.3 %. A checkpoint at the half-life tests the calculation before the final value is accepted. The half-life is the time at which half of the reactant remains, and the half-life follows from the natural logarithm term 0.693 divided by the rate constant, giving 15.4 minutes. Conversion at the half-life is 50 %, and a computed value at the half-life away from that mark signals an error in the exponent. A batch time of 20 minutes gives a product of 0.9 and a conversion of 59.3 %. The shorter batch time gives the lower conversion, and the ordering matches the direction of the mole balance. Unit consistency carries the main risk in the calculation: a rate constant in per minute pairs with time in minutes, and a time entered in hours understates the product and the conversion. Conversion as a percentage and conversion as a fraction describe the same state, and comparison with a specification needs a single form in both places.

points: Flat-sheet membrane with area 12 square metres tested with a dry binary feed of carbon dioxide and nitrogen
Feed pressure 10 bar, permeate pressure 1 bar, test temperature 35 °C
Carbon dioxide permeance 850 GPU and nitrogen permeance 28 GPU; selectivity 30.4
Stage cut 0.25 during the measurement set
Permeate carbon dioxide purity 91 % and carbon dioxide recovery 78 %
Permeance decline over the full test was 4 %
definitions: permeance = permeation flux divided by the partial-pressure difference across the membrane
selectivity = ratio of the permeance of carbon dioxide to the permeance of nitrogen
stage cut = fraction of the feed that passes through the membrane as permeate
prose: Separation of carbon dioxide from nitrogen with a polymer membrane depends on the permeance contrast between the two gases, and membrane performance under mixed-gas feed conditions sets the case for process use. The study measured permeance and selectivity for a flat-sheet membrane with an area of 12 square metres under a dry binary feed. Feed pressure was 10 bar, permeate pressure was 1 bar, and the test temperature was 35 °C. Carbon dioxide permeance, the permeation flux of carbon dioxide divided by its partial-pressure difference across the membrane, reached 850 GPU. Nitrogen permeance was 28 GPU under the same conditions. Selectivity, the ratio of carbon dioxide permeance to nitrogen permeance, was 30.4. Stage cut, the fraction of the feed passing through the membrane as permeate, was held at 0.25 during the measurement set. Permeate purity reached 91 % carbon dioxide, and carbon dioxide recovery reached 78 % of the carbon dioxide in the feed. Permeance decline over the full test was 4 %, and selectivity held within the scatter of the repeat measurements across the test. The pairing of permeate purity with recovery at a single stage cut gives a reference point for module design, and the stability of selectivity during the test supports a longer trial with a membrane module.

points: Shell-and-tube heat exchanger with tube length 3.5 m, tube internal diameter 19 mm and 84 tubes
Water velocity inside the tubes 1.5 m/s
Hot stream inlet temperature 120 °C and cold stream inlet temperature 30 °C
Test duration 500 hours with a measurement set recorded every 24 hours
Clean overall heat transfer coefficient 1250 watts per square metre per kelvin and fouled coefficient 820 watts per square metre per kelvin at the end of the test, a decline of 34.4 %
Fouling resistance at the end of the test 0.00035 square metre kelvin per watt
Uncertainty in fouling resistance 8 %
definitions: overall heat transfer coefficient = heat flow divided by the exchanger area and the logarithmic mean temperature difference, in watts per square metre per kelvin

fouling resistance = deposit resistance computed as the difference between the reciprocal of the fouled overall coefficient and the reciprocal of the clean overall coefficient, in square metre kelvin per watt
limits: Fouling was measured under one water treatment regime; chemical cleaning was not tested
prose: The fouling test used a shell-and-tube heat exchanger with a tube length of 3.5 m, a tube internal diameter of 19 mm and 84 tubes in the bundle. Water flowed inside the tubes at a velocity of 1.5 m/s, and the hot stream entered the shell side. Inlet temperatures were held with the hot stream at 120 °C and the cold stream at 30 °C at entry. The test ran for 500 hours, and the measurement set was recorded every 24 hours across the full run. Each measurement set comprised inlet and outlet temperatures on both streams and the flow rate on each stream, recorded after the temperatures had settled at the set conditions. The overall heat transfer coefficient, the heat flow divided by the exchanger area and the logarithmic mean temperature difference, was computed from each measurement set. The clean overall heat transfer coefficient at the start of the test was 1250 watts per square metre per kelvin. The overall heat transfer coefficient at the end of the test was 820 watts per square metre per kelvin, a decline of 34.4 % from the clean value. Fouling resistance, the deposit resistance computed as the difference between the reciprocal of the fouled overall coefficient and the reciprocal of the clean overall coefficient, reached 0.00035 square metre kelvin per watt at the end of the test. Uncertainty in fouling resistance, propagated from the temperature and flow measurements, was 8 % of the reported value. Cleaning before the test followed a fixed sequence of flushing, brushing of the tube inlets and a final rinse, and the clean coefficient was measured after cleaning and before fouling began. A measurement set was rejected and repeated when the two streams gave heat flows that differed beyond the uncertainty band of the instruments, and the rejection rule was fixed before the test started. Fouling in the test reflects one water treatment regime, and deposit composition was not analysed during the run.

points: Polymer sample from a batch polymerisation with monomer conversion 87 %
Size-exclusion chromatography at 30 °C with sample concentration 1.5 milligrams per millilitre and solvent flow rate 1.0 millilitres per minute
Number-average molar mass 48 kilograms per mole and weight-average molar mass 121 kilograms per mole; dispersity 2.52
Peak molar mass 95 kilograms per mole
Mass fraction below 10 kilograms per mole was 6 %, and mass fraction above 200 kilograms per mole was 9 %
Repeat injections 3 per sample; relative standard deviation of the number-average molar mass 1.8 %
definitions: number-average molar mass = total mass of the sample divided by the total number of molecules, in kilograms per mole
weight-average molar mass = molar mass average weighted by the mass present at each molar mass, in kilograms per mole
dispersity = weight-average molar mass divided by number-average molar mass, dimensionless
size-exclusion chromatography = separation of polymer molecules by size in a packed column, with larger molecules eluting earlier
limits: Molar masses are relative to polystyrene calibration standards and are not absolute values
Distribution covers the soluble fraction of the sample only
figures: Fig. 2: molar mass distribution curve for the polymer sample
prose: The polymer sample came from a batch polymerisation with a monomer conversion of 87 %. Size-exclusion chromatography, a separation of polymer molecules by size in a packed column in which larger molecules elute earlier, gave the molar mass distribution at 30 °C. Sample concentration was 1.5 milligrams per millilitre, and the solvent flow rate was 1.0 millilitres per minute. Fig. 2 shows the molar mass distribution as a single broad peak with a tail on the high-mass side. The number-average molar mass, the total mass of the sample divided by the total number of molecules, was 48 kilograms per mole. The weight-average molar mass, the average weighted by the mass present at each molar mass, was 121 kilograms per mole. Dispersity, the weight-average molar mass divided by the number-average molar mass, was 2.52. The peak molar mass, the molar mass at the maximum of the distribution curve, was 95 kilograms per mole. The mass fraction below 10 kilograms per mole was 6 % of the sample mass. The mass fraction above 200 kilograms per mole was 9 % of the sample mass. The high-mass tail carries the gap between the two averages, since the weight average weights each molecule by the mass at its molar mass, and the tail holds a small count of molecules at a large share of the mass. The low-mass fraction pulls the number average down with the opposite weighting, and the peak sits between the two averages under that pair of pulls. Repeat measurement comprised 3 injections of the sample, and the relative standard deviation of the number-average molar mass was 1.8 %. The molar masses are relative to polystyrene calibration standards rather than absolute values for this polymer, and the distribution covers the soluble fraction of the sample, with any insoluble fraction outside the measurement. A change in the high-mass tail between batches would move the weight average first, and batch comparison on the weight average is the sensitive check for drift in the polymerisation.

points: Influent ammonia concentration 42 milligrams per litre and an effluent target of 2 milligrams per litre, a removal of 95.2 %
Winter wastewater temperature falls to 12 °C
Maximum specific growth rate of the nitrifying organisms 0.6 per day at the reference condition
Full-scale solids retention time 6 days against a required retention time of 9 days at low temperature
Pilot reactor volume 300 litres
Dissolved oxygen set point 2.5 milligrams per litre in the pilot reactor, with effluent ammonia 1.8 milligrams per litre
Knowledge gap: nitrification rates at low temperature in full-scale plants receiving mixed industrial input
definitions: nitrification = biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrite and then to nitrate by nitrifying organisms
solids retention time = average time that biomass stays in the reactor, in days
ammonia concentration = mass of ammonia nitrogen per unit volume of wastewater, in milligrams per litre
limits: Design values in the plant record rest on laboratory rates with a synthetic feed
prose: Nitrification, the biological oxidation of ammonia to nitrite and then to nitrate by nitrifying organisms, carries the ammonia load of municipal wastewater in the activated sludge process. Influent ammonia concentration in the plant record is 42 milligrams per litre, and the discharge consent sets an effluent target of 2 milligrams per litre. The gap between influent and target is a removal of 95.2 %, and removal at that depth leaves a small margin for a process upset. Winter operation sets the hard case for the plant. Wastewater temperature falls to 12 °C in winter, and the maximum specific growth rate of the nitrifying organisms falls with temperature from the reference value of 0.6 per day. Solids retention time, the average time that biomass stays in the reactor, is 6 days in the full-scale plant. The required retention time at low temperature is 9 days, and the plant value sits below the required value in the season with the slowest growth. Published rates for nitrification at low temperature come mainly from laboratory reactors with a synthetic feed, and rates in full-scale plants with a mixed industrial input are not established. The study addresses that gap with a pilot reactor of 300 litres fed from the plant inlet across a winter season. Dissolved oxygen in the pilot reactor was held at a set point of 2.5 milligrams per litre, and effluent ammonia from the pilot reactor reached 1.8 milligrams per litre in the coldest period. The pilot record gives a rate and a retention time from the same feed that the full-scale plant treats, and the comparison with the full-scale record forms the test of the design values.

points: Treated device efficiency 24.6 % and control device efficiency 21.3 %
Sample size 18 devices in each group
Standard deviation 0.7 percentage points for the treated group and 1.1 percentage points for the control group
Active area 0.16 square centimetres
Illumination 100 milliwatts per square centimetre from a solar simulator
definitions: power conversion efficiency = electrical power output divided by incident light power, as a percentage
current density = current divided by active area
limits: Efficiency values are from reverse voltage scans
figures: Fig. 3: current density against voltage for treated and control perovskite solar cells
prose: Fig. 3 | Power conversion efficiency of perovskite solar cells with a surface treatment and of control cells without the treatment. Current density, the current divided by the active area, against voltage under simulated sunlight at 100 milliwatts per square centimetre, for devices with an active area of 0.16 square centimetres. Treated cells reached a power conversion efficiency, the electrical power output divided by the incident light power, of 24.6 %, and control cells reached 21.3 %. Each group held 18 devices, and the standard deviation of efficiency was 0.7 percentage points for the treated group and 1.1 percentage points for the control group. Efficiency values come from reverse voltage scans.

points: Pipe length 15 m and pipe internal diameter 0.05 m; length divided by diameter 300
Water density 998 kilograms per cubic metre and dynamic viscosity 0.001 pascal seconds
Mean velocity 1.8 m/s; velocity squared 3.24
Reynolds number 89820 for the stated conditions
Friction factor 0.021 from the Colebrook relation for a smooth pipe wall
Friction factor multiplied by the length-to-diameter ratio gives 6.3
Computed pressure drop 10.2 kPa
Velocity term in the equation is the density multiplied by the velocity squared and divided by 2
definitions: ΔP = pressure drop across the pipe length, in pascals
f = Darcy friction factor, dimensionless
L = pipe length, in metres
D = pipe internal diameter, in metres
ρ = fluid density, in kilograms per cubic metre
v = mean velocity of the fluid in the pipe, in metres per second
μ = dynamic viscosity of the fluid, in pascal seconds
Re = Reynolds number, density multiplied by velocity and diameter and divided by dynamic viscosity, dimensionless
limits: Equation applies to steady, incompressible, fully developed flow in a straight circular pipe
Friction factor value applies to turbulent flow over a smooth pipe wall
prose: Pressure drop in a straight circular pipe follows the Darcy–Weisbach equation, stated here in prose with each symbol defined in the order of first use. The symbol ΔP is the pressure drop across the pipe length, in pascals, and the symbol f is the Darcy friction factor, a dimensionless factor that carries the wall resistance. The symbol L is the pipe length, in metres, and the symbol D is the pipe internal diameter, in metres. The symbol ρ is the fluid density, in kilograms per cubic metre, and the symbol v is the mean velocity, in metres per second. The equation states that ΔP equals f multiplied by the ratio of L to D, multiplied by ρ multiplied by the square of v and divided by 2. The symbol μ is the dynamic viscosity, in pascal seconds, and the symbol Re is the Reynolds number, the product ρ v D divided by μ, which sets the flow regime. The worked case uses water in a pipe with L of 15 m and D of 0.05 m, and the ratio of L to D is 300. Density ρ is 998 kilograms per cubic metre, dynamic viscosity μ is 0.001 pascal seconds, and mean velocity v is 1.8 m/s. The square of v is 3.24, and the Reynolds number is 89820, in the turbulent range. The Colebrook relation for a smooth pipe wall gives f of 0.021 at that Reynolds number, and the product of f and the length-to-diameter ratio is 6.3. The equation gives a pressure drop ΔP of 10.2 kPa for the case. The equation holds for steady, incompressible, fully developed flow in a straight circular pipe, and fittings and entrance lengths sit outside the stated length. Laminar flow follows a different friction factor relation, with f varying inversely with Re, and the turbulent value does not carry into that regime.
